typing like I’m running out of time cause I’m actually running out of time.First, full disclosure: I’m not Japanese.
I’ve never worked for a Japanese company, and I definitely don’t have that aesthetic life where I wake up at 5 AM, drink green tea, and write flawless code while some lo-fi anime beat plays in the background. I wish.
In reality, I’m just a programmer who spends way too much time staring at a screen, gets hyped about a new framework, and then somehow ends up watching YouTube videos about “productivity” instead of actually doing any work. Standard dev behavior.
But at some point, I started getting into Japanese work culture. Not because I thought there was some secret cheat code to suddenly become a “10x engineer” (I tried that — buying a fancy mechanical keyboard doesn’t actually make you better at coding, I learned that the hard way). I was just interested because I noticed that a lot of their principles aren’t about grinding harder, but more about respecting the process.
As programmers, we’re always fighting ourselves. We want to be seniors immediately, build a massive startup, and know every single language and LeetCode problem. Then we get overwhelmed, do nothing for three days, and feel like trash.
So, I tried out some Japanese-inspired habits. Some were a total fail, but here are the ones that actually worked for me.
1. Kaizen: Just Getting Slightly Better
Kaizen is basically “small, continuous improvement.” At first, I was like, “That’s it?” Because we love overcomplicating things. We want a complex algorithm or a 37-step Notion template to fix our lives.
But Kaizen is just… annoyingly simple. Just get a little better every day.
For my coding, this changed everything. Instead of saying “I need to be a pro software engineer by the end of the year,” I started asking, “What can I actually improve today?” Maybe I learn one React hook, solve one easy LeetCode problem, or fix some ugly code I wrote yesterday.
It’s boring, but doing that consistently actually works. Nobody cares if you spent 30 minutes studying arrays, but those small wins eventually stack up.
2. Shokunin: Treating it Like a Craft
Shokunin is the idea of craftsmanship — basically, deeply respecting what you do. When I first heard this, I imagined some master dev in a quiet room writing perfect code. Then I looked at my own projects, which honestly look like they were written by a sleep-deprived raccoon.
But the point is that programming isn’t just typing; it’s a craft. A good dev cares about the small stuff — variable naming, readable functions, and actually understanding why something works instead of just copy-pasting from StackOverflow.
I started looking at my old projects differently. Instead of being embarrassed by my old code, I realized that if it looks bad now, it means I’ve actually improved since then.
3. Hara Hachi Bu: Don’t Burn Out
This one is basically about moderation. Hara Hachi Bu is the idea of eating until you’re only 80% full.
Programmers desperately need this because our default mode is: “Work 12 hours, learn five languages, and become a senior dev by next Tuesday.” Then three days later, we’re burnt out, hating programming, and wondering if we’re even talented.
I’ve done this so many times. The problem wasn’t my ambition; it was my system. Programming is a marathon. If you run your laptop at 100% CPU forever, it crashes. Why do we think we’re different?
4. Mottainai: Stop Wasting Your Focus
Mottainai is about avoiding waste — not just food or materials, but opportunities. For us, I think that means attention.
Our attention is our biggest resource, and we waste it constantly. You open Instagram for “one second,” check YouTube, read a random article, and suddenly three hours are gone.
I started treating my focus as something valuable. Not every notification needs a reply, and not every new JS framework is worth my time. Sometimes the most productive thing you can do is just ignore the noise.
5. Doing the Work When Nobody is Watching
A lot of Japanese craftsmanship is about quality, even if no one sees it. This is hard when you’re a beginner because we want visible progress — like “I built five projects” or “I learned ten technologies.”
But the real growth happens in the invisible parts: reading the actual documentation, fighting with error messages for two hours, and refactoring code. Nobody sees that, but that’s what actually separates an average dev from a strong one.
The Reality
Did this turn me into some legendary programmer? No. I still procrastinate, I still get stuck on stupid bugs, and I still look at code I wrote yesterday and think, “Who wrote this garbage?” (Then I remember it was me).
But it changed my approach. I stopped looking for shortcuts and stopped waiting for “motivation” to hit. I just focus on small improvements. One concept, one bug fix, one day at a time.
The “magic” isn’t in the habits themselves — it’s just consistency. Programming isn’t won in one huge moment; it’s won in the thousands of small moments where you decide to get 1% better.
And honestly, that’s the closest thing we have to a cheat code.
